intro_html:
HB 5764 has sat in the House Energy Committee since March 2026, and bills still pending when the Legislature’s two-year session ends in December 2026 die. Until something passes, the Michigan Public Service Commission’s position is short: “Prior to operating a distributed generation project, a customer must properly interconnect the project with the utility,” which in Detroit means DTE Electric.

Michigan does have a recent solar-access law, the Homeowners Energy Policy Act (2024 PA 68), in force since April 2025. It voids homeowners association rules that prohibit, or have the effect of prohibiting, a solar energy system, and lets the owner go ahead if the association has not decided an application within 30 days. It does not apply in a “common area”, defined as space “generally accessible to all members”, or on a shared roof, so a private balcony is not excluded on that ground. But the act never defines “homeowners association”, and at least one Michigan community-association law firm reads it as not reaching condominium co-owner associations, so its reach to a condo balcony is unsettled. It covers owners only.

DTE’s standard residential rate is time-of-day: from June to September a weekday kWh between 3 and 7 p.m. costs 24.1¢ in supply and distribution charges against 18.4¢ at other times, before surcharges, and a west-facing railing does more of its work in those hours than a south-facing one. balco.nyc’s calculator lets you enter the rate from your own bill.

faq: Does Michigan's Homeowners Energy Policy Act apply to condominiums?

It is unclear. The act (2024 PA 68) voids homeowners association rules that prohibit solar energy systems and gives associations 30 days to decide an application, but it never defines “homeowners association”, and at least one Michigan community-association law firm reads it as not covering condominium co-owner associations. It does not apply in common areas generally accessible to all members or on shared roofs.
